drills.q: Walk through the three-way handshake with actual sequence number arithmetic for client ISN=1000, server ISN=5000, then a subsequent 200-byte data send.
drills.a: SYN(seq=1000) -> SYN-ACK(seq=5000, ack=1001) -> ACK(ack=5001). A following 200-byte data segment carries seq=1001, acked as ack=1201 (1001+200). SYN/FIN each consume one sequence number; bare ACKs consume none.

drills.q: List all 11 TCP states and identify which two are most commonly confused/misdiagnosed in production.
drills.a: CLOSED, LISTEN, SYN_SENT, SYN_RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN_WAIT_1, FIN_WAIT_2, CLOSE_WAIT, CLOSING, LAST_ACK, TIME_WAIT. CLOSE_WAIT (mistaken for a network issue when it's an app bug) and TIME_WAIT (mistaken for something tunable via a documented sysctl when its duration is hardcoded).

drills.q: A server has 5,000 sockets stuck in CLOSE_WAIT. What's your first hypothesis and why?
drills.a: An application resource leak -- the peer sent FIN (kernel acked it), but some code path in the app (very often an exception path) never calls close(). This is essentially never a network problem; checking kernel tunables first wastes the incident.

drills.q: Explain both reasons TIME_WAIT exists, and state its actual duration on Linux vs the RFC 793 theoretical value.
drills.a: 1) Absorbs a delayed duplicate segment from this exact connection so it can't be misdelivered into a new connection reusing the same 4-tuple. 2) Keeps state around long enough to retransmit the final ACK if the peer's LAST_ACK-state FIN retransmission arrives because the original ACK was lost. RFC 793 theory: 2xMSL, MSL=2min -> 4 minutes. Linux reality: hardcoded flat 60 seconds (TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN), not tunable via sysctl.

drills.q: A server under high connection churn is running out of ephemeral ports. Diagnose and fix, and explain why tcp_tw_recycle is the wrong answer.
drills.a: High-churn outbound connections pin ports in TIME_WAIT for 60s each, exhausting the ~28,000-port default ephemeral range. Fix: enable tcp_tw_reuse (safe, client-side port recycling using timestamps), but the durable fix is reducing churn via pooling/keep-alive. tcp_tw_recycle is removed from the kernel (4.12+) because its safety check assumed monotonically increasing per-peer timestamps, which is false behind NAT where multiple clients share a source IP -- it silently drops legitimate NATed connections.

drills.q: Differentiate FIN and RST, and explain exactly when the kernel sends RST instead of a graceful close.
drills.a: FIN is a graceful, ordered 'no more from me, still can receive' signal, part of the normal handshake/teardown state machine, consuming one sequence number. RST is an abrupt abort with no delivery guarantee. The kernel sends RST instead of FIN when an application calls close() on a socket that still has unread data in its receive buffer -- a clean close would silently discard that data, so RST signals the abnormal termination instead, producing the classic 'Connection reset by peer' error.

drills.q: At 10Gbps, how long until TCP sequence numbers wrap, and what mechanism protects against misinterpreting a wrapped duplicate as new data?
drills.a: 2^32 bytes x 8 bits / 10e9 bits/sec ~= 3.4 seconds. PAWS (Protection Against Wrapped Sequence numbers, RFC 7323) uses the TCP timestamp option -- a monotonically increasing value on every segment -- to disambiguate an old wrapped-around duplicate from legitimate new data once raw sequence numbers alone can no longer be trusted at that speed.

drills.q: Explain a half-close with a real use case, and identify what TCP state the initiating side is in while still able to receive.
drills.a: A half-close is shutdown(SHUT_WR): one side sends FIN (no more data from me) while the connection stays open in the other direction. Real use case: a client uploading a large body calls shutdown(SHUT_WR) after finishing the upload, then reads the server's response on the same connection. The initiating side sits in FIN_WAIT_2 (after its FIN is acked) and can still receive data -- that's the entire point of the half-close.

drills.q: Two hosts send FIN to each other at nearly the same time. Trace the state transitions on both sides.
drills.a: Simultaneous close: both move ESTABLISHED -> FIN_WAIT_1 on sending their own FIN. Each then receives the other's FIN before receiving an ACK of its own, transitioning FIN_WAIT_1 -> CLOSING (instead of the usual FIN_WAIT_2 path), sends an ACK for the peer's FIN, and once that ACK is received both move to TIME_WAIT and eventually CLOSED. Unlike the normal asymmetric close, BOTH peers pass through TIME_WAIT here.

drills.q: An RTO-based retransmission is set with Linux defaults. How long, worst case, before the kernel reports a genuinely dead connection as failed, and why is this insufficient for a user-facing system?
drills.a: Initial RTO=1s (RFC 6298), exponential backoff per retransmit, tcp_retries2 default=15 -> roughly 15-30 minutes worst case before the kernel gives up and reports failure to the application. This is unacceptable for anything user-facing, which is why application-level timeouts and circuit breakers sit on top of TCP's own retry behavior rather than relying on it as the failure-detection mechanism.
